title: Cross-compilation: `GOOS`, `GOARCH` and a binary for another machine

videos.script: A Go program usually runs somewhere other than the laptop it was written on. A server with an ARM processor, a colleague's Mac, a Windows desktop. This lesson builds hits for all of them, from one machine. {{vars}} Two environment variables do it. GOOS names the operating system and GOARCH names the processor. Set them, run go build, and out comes a binary for that machine. There is no second compiler to install, because the Go toolchain is written in Go. {{qemu}} Then the ARM binary has to prove it works. This machine cannot run it, so an emulator does, and its table matches the native one to the last digit. The tests pass on it too. {{breaks}} Next, what changes with the target. Cross builds turn cgo off, so a program that calls C stops building. A package can pick different files for each system. And a binary built for a newer processor refuses to start on an older one. You will see that refusal happen. {{release}} Last, a short script builds six binaries for three systems, each named for where it runs. Lessons 17 and 18 shrink them and ship them.
